corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the open-source prediction follows 'one other thing bill is I'm just thinking about 2025 predictions', so it is Brad Gerstner speaking to Bill.
corrections.fix: Brad Gerstner: expect more companies to open-source models in 2025 (e.g. Microsoft), as major AI players share more common ground than division.

corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the ~$300bn non-governmental R&D / Bell Labs point continues Brad's answer on co-opetition; only the remark that big tech had been criticised for buybacks but now has a use for cash is Bill's.
corrections.fix: Brad Gerstner: almost $300bn of big-tech AI R&D/capex funded from cash flow is bullish for the US strategic position (like Bell Labs); Bill adds this answers earlier criticism that the firms only did buybacks.

corrections.issue: Mixed speakers: the point that falling compute prices encourage running many passes was Bill's, not Brad's.
corrections.fix: Brad Gerstner: reasoning models improve with more test-time compute; labs say they are around a 'GPT-2' stage of log scaling, so big gains are expected in 2025-2026. (Bill: falling compute prices make many passes per task worthwhile.)

corrections.issue: Merges two speakers: the 'Google as the perfect AI basket of assets (Gmail, Docs, Android)' thesis was Bill's; Brad's reply was the innovator's dilemma of replacing a 99% incremental margin search monopoly.
corrections.fix: Bill: Google's assets (Workspace, Android, search) could be the ideal AI bundle. Brad: Google faces the largest innovator's dilemma, replacing a 99% incremental-margin search monopoly with lower-margin AI; it could win if Gemini displaces Apple's assistant on phones.

completeness_estimate: 0.70 - first reader got the macro/valuation/fiscal core and main AI capex points, but missed several investable mechanisms (capex recipients, consensus-vs-capex check, cyclical multiple rule, capex intensity warning), speaker disagreements, and had four speaker attribution errors (captions lack speaker cues).
